outcome: The conjecture itself (infinitely many palindromic primes in every base) remains unresolved; only weaker/adjacent statements about palindromes with restricted factorizations have been proven since January 2024.
summary: The bullet asks whether there are infinitely many palindromic primes in every base — an existence/infinitude question that, per §3.1, moves only when actually answered. It has not been answered. The Wikipedia article on palindromic primes (fetched at its current, live state) still says plainly that it is not known whether there are infinitely many palindromic primes even in base 10, and the conjecture for general bases is described in the literature as 'far out of reach with current methods,' the sparsity of palindromes (~√x below x) being the core obstruction. Since 26 January 2024 there has been a cluster of closely related but genuinely distinct results, each of which changes the question rather than the problem in this bullet: (1) Tuxanidy and Panario, 'Infinitude of Palindromic Almost-Prime Numbers' (arXiv:2307.16637, first submitted 31 July 2023 — before the window — with a revised v3 posted 23 July 2024 and journal publication in IMRN in September 2024), proving infinitely many palindromes in any base with at most six prime factors, each large; this is a genuine mathematical advance but is explicitly a weakening (almost-primes, not primes) that the authors themselves note their methods cannot push to square-free palindromes, let alone primes. (2) Johnston and Kerr, 'The infinitude of square-free palindromes' (arXiv:2601.07097, dated January 2026), proving infinitely many square-free palindromes in every base — again a different, weaker statement (no primality). (3) Chourasiya and Johnston, 'Power-free palindromes and reversed primes' (arXiv:2503.21136), which studies power-free palindromes and reversed-prime variants, not the stated conjecture. None of these settle any case of, or move a bound on, the actual conjecture that palindromic primes (not almost-primes, not square-free palindromes) are infinite in a given base — they are all related problems under §3.1's test, obtained by relaxing 'prime' to a weaker multiplicative condition, not by restricting the original statement. No AI system was found credited in any of these papers' methodology, acknowledgements, or metadata; all read as conventional analytic/combinatorial number theory. A broader search for any AI-driven attempt on this specific conjecture (e.g. via LLM theorem-proving pipelines, AI agents solving Erdős-style problem lists) turned up general AI-for-math activity (e.g. AI agents resolving some Erdős problems and OEIS conjectures) but nothing naming or touching this palindromic-primes conjecture. The triage's 'none' verdict is confirmed: this problem saw real progress in its neighborhood but no change to the bullet as stated, and no AI involvement anywhere in that neighborhood.
competing_reading: One could argue the almost-prime result (at most six prime factors) is a 'case' of the palindromic-primes conjecture in the loose sense that primes are almost-primes with exactly one factor, so the almost-prime result narrows the search space. But per §3.1 a case is obtained by *restricting* the stated question (e.g., a specific base, a specific digit length), not by *relaxing* the primality condition to a different, strictly weaker multiplicative condition; six-almost-primes are not a subset of primes, so proving infinitude of the former says nothing about whether primes among palindromes are finite or infinite. I classify all three papers as related-problem territory, not partial progress on this bullet, but flag the reasoning here since a differently-calibrated reader might score the almost-prime result as `partial`.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that for some fixed base b, the number of palindromic primes below x is unbounded (or is eventually zero) would resolve the case for that base; a paper explicitly closing the gap from 'six prime factors' to 'one prime factor' for palindromes, or any result stated in terms of prime palindromes themselves (not almost-primes or square-free palindromes), would be the marker to search for going forward.
